key_insight: Vision-language pretraining does not consistently make text representations more human-like: VLMs do not show a global advantage over matched LLMs in aligning with human natural reading behavior, with benefits that are mixed and context-dependent.
problem_solved: Clarifies whether multimodal (vision-language) training histories improve how model text representations match human reading processes, isolating the effect of multimodal pretraining from visual input or cross-modal fusion.
method: Construct tightly matched model pairs (same architecture/config except for multimodal vs text-only pretraining) to isolate training-history effects.
Evaluate all models in a strictly text-only setting so no online visual input or fusion affects results.
Compare model representations to human natural-reading measurements (e.g., behavioral/eye-tracking or neural benchmarks) and analyze global vs. local alignment differences.
impact: Warns practitioners that multimodal pretraining is not a guaranteed shortcut to improved human-aligned text representations; alignment should be validated per task and dataset rather than assumed from VLM training.
visual_elements: Schematic of matched-model pairs: side-by-side LLM vs VLM with identical architecture but different pretraining history.
Bar/violin chart comparing alignment scores (LLM vs VLM) showing no consistent global advantage for VLMs and task/context-dependent differences.
Heatmap or token-wise plot illustrating where VLMs outperform/underperform LLMs across reading timepoints or text positions.
Pipeline flowchart: data → matched models → text-only evaluation → human benchmark comparison → alignment analysis.
paper_title: VLMs May Not Globally Enhance Human Alignment over LLMs During Natural Reading
paper_authors: Jinzhou Wu, Zhengwu Ma, Jixing Li, Baoping Tang, Zitong Lu
